newsitem.title: JAPAN: Aussie, beset by rate fears, languishes vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Aussie, beset by rate fears, languishes vs yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar, beset by concerns about a possible interest rate cut, languished at the lower end of 97 yen on Monday and could even slip lower, Tokyo dealers said.

"The Aussie's failure to break above 100 yen two weeks ago disappointed the market, turning buyers to sellers. Now it has become gradually more sensitive to bad news," a dealer at an Australian bank said.
He and other dealers said that with a key wage claims verdict due on Tuesday and first-quarter consumer price data on Wednesday, the short-term outlook was unclear but bearish.

Concern about a rate cut has risen since jobs figures in March showed a second consecutive drop. Rates were last changed on December 11 when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), in a shock move, took the key cash rate down to 6.00 percent.
Dealers noted that with a U.S. rate rise widely expected later this year, a cut in Australian rates would broaden the interest rate differential between the two countries.
Concern about this has combined with the current lack of direction in the U.S. dollar's moves against the yen to reduce investors' appetite for the Aussie, they added.

"Prospects of a U.S. rate hike and the directionless dollar/yen trade are both eating away at the flow of capital into the Aussie. There's a lot of selling interest right now," said a dealer with a different Australian bank.
"The biggest negative factor is definitely the chance of a U.S. rate hike. If the Fed would abandon the idea of raising rates, the Aussie would start to gain again," he added.

He said sentiment for the Aussie was likely to be bearish for the next two weeks, with slides down to the 95.50 to 96.00 yen level likely. But bargain-hunting would stop further dips and the longer-term outlook may become more bullish, he added.

He said the Aussie could even take another shot at 100 yen after this downward correction and added that a rate cut was unlikely soon. "At this point it is still too early to see the full impact of the previous three cuts," he said.
But the first dealer said that should the annual underlying rate in the consumer price data come in at less than the expected 2.1 percent, talk about a rate cut would increase.

The second dealer noted that while some Japanese investors appeared to have sold the Aussie in connection with Japan's fiscal year-end on March 31, the early part of April saw buying pick up a bit as the new fiscal year invited fresh investment.
About 150 billion yen worth of yen/Australian dollar dual currency bonds have been issued since January, including one reverse dual-currency samurai.
But the first dealer said that with interest now shifting more to short-term dollar investments, the appetite for these was likely to be limited.
The Aussie stood near 97.46/56 yen by late Tokyo, unchanged from early trade, after recovering from a dip to around 97.13 yen. It ended Friday Tokyo trade near 97.68/78 yen.
